synopsis: RL Token (RLT) specializes a pretrained VLA through a compact representation and a small online actor–critic. A reconstruction-trained token supplies perceptual context, while sampled VLA actions guide useful refinements. Physical-robot experiments show faster critical phases and improved reliability, but rely on task demonstrations, human supervision, and carefully separated critical-phase and full-task evaluations. [e-token, e-policy, e-evaluation, e-results, e-human]

problem.text: Precision manipulation can fail during final alignment or contact even when a VLA handles the preceding task. The paper seeks online improvement within limited robot interaction budgets, combining pretrained perception and behavior with the sample efficiency of small off-policy learners.

contributions.text: A learned RL token compresses VLA embeddings through autoregressive reconstruction; online RL freezes this interface and the VLA.

Reference-conditioned action chunks, a quadratic policy anchor, and reference dropout support lightweight refinement. Experiments cover screw installation, zip tie fastening, Ethernet insertion, and charger insertion.

inputs: Two wrist-camera images and one base-camera image in the experiments; a fixed task instruction for the VLA.
RL token, proprioceptive state, and a sampled VLA reference-action prefix for the actor.
outputs: A Gaussian distribution over ten-step, 14-dimensional actions: a 140-dimensional RL chunk.
A critic estimate for a state and action chunk; executed actions produce subsequent robot observations.

steps.name: Expose the representation
steps.detail: The encoder appends a learned readout embedding to final-layer VLA tokens. Its output at that position becomes the 2048-dimensional RL token. The decoder reconstructs VLA embeddings autoregressively with stopped-gradient targets. Tasks use fixed instructions, so language embeddings are omitted from this compression step.

steps.name: Refine a proposal
steps.detail: The frozen VLA predicts 50 actions. The actor uses the RL token, proprioception, and the first ten reference actions to propose a complete refined chunk; it does not predict an additive residual. The sampled reference supplies information about the VLA behavior mode.

steps.name: Learn from executed transitions
steps.detail: VLA warmup, actor rollouts, and optional teleoperated corrections enter replay. An intervention replaces both the executed action and stored reference. A chunk-level temporal-difference target propagates sparse terminal success reward; the physical environment supplies the next observation.

training.text: Per task, 1–10 hours of demonstrations support VLA fine-tuning and token training; Appendix B gives 2,000–10,000 gradient steps. Online RL then freezes both modules. The reported 400–1,000 training episodes yield approximately 15 minutes to five hours of robot data, excluding resets and other overhead.

Actor and critic start from scratch. Appendix B specifies a two-layer MLP with hidden dimension 256 for zip tie, Ethernet, and charger, and a three-layer MLP with hidden dimension 512 for screw. It does not define the layer-count convention, so these are not established hidden-layer counts. Two critics supply the minimum target value. Reference input is zeroed on 50% of training samples; Gaussian noise has a small fixed, unspecified standard deviation.

Rollouts and learning are asynchronous, with two critic updates per actor update and an update-to-data ratio of five. Overlapping chunks are stored every two control steps. Operators label success, may correct behavior, and choose the critical-phase handoff.

inference.text: At chunk boundaries, obtain fresh context and a VLA reference, then execute ten actor actions at 50 Hz before replanning. Reference dropout is disabled. The VLA handles easier phases. Section V describes an optional final supervised VLA fine-tune to predict handoff from human labels; switch accuracy is not quantified.

equations.explanation: Equation (1): z denotes final-layer VLA embeddings, M their count, e_rl the learned readout, and g_phi the encoder. The appended-position output is the RL token. Equation (2) trains a decoder to reconstruct stopped-gradient embeddings from that token and preceding targets.

Equation (3): C is chunk length, gamma the discount, r reward, x the token plus proprioception, and x′ the next chunk state. The target critic has parameters psi′; the actor samples the next chunk a′. Critic training minimizes squared error to this target.

Equation (5): the actor maximizes critic value while beta weights closeness to the VLA reference. B is replay, s the observation, and ell the instruction. The reference is both an input and a regularization target, not a hard action constraint.

results.setting: Physical robot; slightly randomized starts immediately before the critical phase. Section VI-A specifies 50 evaluation episodes per agent and task.
results.interpretation: The introduction states these values; Figure 5 places the comparison outside the full-task box. The reported difference is 45 percentage points. Raw counts and the meaning of plotted error bars are not supplied.

results.setting: Figure 9 compares the final policy with the base VLA and expert teleoperated demonstrations on the insertion segment.
results.metric: Median episode length, control timesteps; lower is faster
results.interpretation: The directly labeled medians support faster insertion than either comparator. They are not full-task timings or the mean-completion statistic discussed elsewhere.

results.task: Ethernet insertion — comparison with other learning methods
results.setting: Controlled critical-phase protocol; authors state equal data amounts for RL methods.
results.metric: Success rate and successful completions per ten minutes
results.value: RLT has the highest plotted throughput, with near-ceiling success.
results.comparison: DAgger and DSRL have comparable high success but lower throughput; PLD and HIL-SERL perform worse in this implementation.
results.interpretation: The comparison is confined to Ethernet. Appendix C notes HIL-SERL runs at 50 Hz here versus its original 10 Hz and lacks its action-space bounding box.

results.setting: Figure 7 evaluates successive checkpoints against minutes of collected critical-phase data.
results.metric: Throughput, successful completions per ten minutes
results.value: RLT exceeds the base policy by five minutes of data; the caption reports about 40 minutes total experiment time.
results.comparison: Removing reference pass-through slows early learning but eventually reaches similar throughput. Removing the BC regularizer gives the largest failure.
results.interpretation: No seed uncertainty is reported. The single-step variant also changes the encoder, so it does not isolate chunk length.

limitations.text: Training still needs human reward labels, corrections, and handoff decisions. Controlled trials start near the bottleneck; full-task testing covers only screw and zip tie. These results do not establish unattended improvement or broad transfer to unseen tasks.

The no-chunk ablation also substitutes ResNet-10, confounding horizon and representation. Section VI-C says removing the token reduces throughput by 50%, while Figure 7 endpoints are approximately 150 versus 400; the paper does not reconcile this difference.

No results table, raw trial counts, seed count, or definition of plotted error bars is supplied. Section VI-C describes full-task gains as 40% and 60% without specifying relative change versus percentage points; this report does not convert those phrases into precise estimates.

reproduction.text: Reproduction needs the specified VLA, task demonstrations, camera/proprioceptive interfaces, 50 Hz control, human labels, and staged critical-phase/full-task training. Missing settings include beta and gamma values, learning rates, exact warmup budget, noise magnitude, token-transformer depth, and training hardware. Appendix B also leaves the MLP layer-count convention unspecified. These are implementation gaps, not evidence of failed reproduction.

Proposed checks should separate representation from chunk length and test reference dropout under matched supervision. Record interaction and elapsed time. Algorithm 1 stores next states using t+1 although Equation (3) and Section III specify C-step backups; implementation must resolve that indexing explicitly.

reasoning.text: The VLA and separately trained online actor–critic support the recorded Dual-system VLA post-training classification. Reconstructing current internal embeddings is auxiliary training. The method predicts actions and return, without a future-observation world model or inverse-dynamics action extraction; the world/action prediction quadrant is therefore not applicable.

discussionQuestions: Does the RL token retain a benefit when encoder capacity, data, and action horizon are matched? [e-ablation]
How much practical improvement survives automated rewards and handoffs under full-task starts? [e-human, e-handoff, e-evaluation]

evidence.location: PDF p. 1, title, author block, affiliation, and arXiv margin stamp
evidence.detail: The observed title credits Charles Xu, Jost Tobias Springenberg, Michael Equi, Ali Amin, Adnan Esmail, Sergey Levine, and Liyiming Ke at Physical Intelligence; the stamp identifies 2604.23073v2, 30 April 2026.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 1–3, Sections I and IV opening
evidence.detail: Precision-critical execution motivates a compact frozen-VLA interface for sample-efficient online actor–critic learning.

evidence.location: PDF p. 3, Section III, VLA and RL preliminaries
evidence.detail: The VLA predicts H=50 actions; RL uses C<H. The chunk-level value expression bootstraps from state t+C. Reward is a human-labeled terminal success/failure signal.

evidence.location: PDF p. 4, Figure 2, Section IV-A, Eqs. (1)–(2), footnote 1
evidence.detail: The encoder extracts a 1×2048 readout. Autoregressive reconstruction uses stopped-gradient VLA embeddings. Language embeddings are omitted for fixed-instruction tasks; VLA and readout are frozen for online RL.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 4–5, Section IV-B, Eqs. (3)–(5) and Reference action dropout
evidence.detail: The state is the RL token plus proprioception. A Gaussian actor conditions on a VLA reference, maximizes chunk critic value with a quadratic anchor, and receives zero reference inputs on some training transitions.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 5–6, Section V, Algorithm 1 and Warmup/Rollout/Subsampling/Update paragraphs
evidence.detail: Replay includes warmup, autonomous, and human actions; corrections replace stored references. Chunks use stride two. Updates are asynchronous, with two critic updates per actor update and update-to-data ratio five. Algorithm lines 10–12 use t+1 notation despite chunk execution.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Section V, Targeted improvement of critical phases
evidence.detail: Operators select handoff and terminal outcome. An optional final supervised VLA fine-tune can learn handoff prediction from intervention labels.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 6–7, Figure 3 and Section VI-A, task descriptions and Experiment Details
evidence.detail: Four tasks involve screw, zip tie, Ethernet, and charger manipulation. Experiments use two wrist views, one base view, proprioception, 50 Hz control, and 14-dimensional actions forming a 140-dimensional RL chunk.

evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Section VI-B; p. 12, Appendix B
evidence.detail: Task demonstrations span 1–10 hours; online runs span 400–1,000 episodes and 15 minutes to five hours of data excluding overhead. Initial adaptation uses 2,000–10,000 gradient steps; harder-task policies are reported after about five hours of data.

evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Section VI-A, Critical-phase evaluation and Full-task evaluation; Section VI-B
evidence.detail: Controlled evaluation uses slightly randomized partially completed states and 50 episodes per agent/task. Full-task evaluations start at home and cover screw and zip tie. Metrics are success and successful completions per ten minutes.

evidence.location: PDF p. 2, Section I, first results paragraph; p. 8, Figures 4–5 and Section VI-C Q1
evidence.detail: The introduction reports screw success rising from 20% to 65%; Figure 5 places that comparison in the critical-phase setting. Figures 4–5 show throughput/success across tasks. Q1 labels full-task gains 40% and 60%, without defining the percentage convention.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 7–8, Section VI-B baseline definitions; p. 8, Figure 6 and Section VI-C Q2
evidence.detail: The Ethernet comparison shows higher RLT throughput than DAgger, HIL-SERL, PLD, and DSRL. DAgger and DSRL reach similarly high success. Authors state matched data amounts for RL methods.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 7–9, Section VI-B ablation definitions and Section VI-C Q3; p. 9, Figures 7–8 and captions
evidence.detail: No-chunk also replaces the token with ResNet-10. Removing pass-through slows learning; removing regularization fails. Figure 7 reports five minutes of data versus about 40 minutes total experiment time. Q3 claims 50% token-ablation throughput loss, whereas final plotted values are around 150 versus 400.

evidence.location: PDF p. 9, Figure 9 median labels, caption, and Section VI-C Q4
evidence.detail: Ethernet insertion medians are RLT 66, teleoperation 146, base policy 228 timesteps. Authors describe less probing and emergent pressing/wiggling; the caption confines the distribution to critical insertion.

evidence.location: PDF p. 9, Section VII, limitations paragraph
evidence.detail: Human reward labels, intervention corrections, and switching remain required during training; reward/progress models and a fully autonomous pipeline are future directions.

evidence.location: PDF p. 12, Appendix B, all paragraphs
evidence.detail: Appendix B specifies a two-layer MLP with hidden dimension 256 for zip tie, Ethernet, and charger, and a three-layer MLP with hidden dimension 512 for screw. It does not say whether output layers count toward these depths. Two critics use the minimum target. Reference dropout is 50% during training and absent at inference. C=10, stride two, fixed small Gaussian noise, and staged harder-task training are specified. Exact optimizer, noise magnitude, and hardware settings are absent.

PLD critic pretraining uses 50 base-policy rollouts and Cal-QL. DSRL repeats a 1×32 latent 50 times. HIL-SERL starts with 20 demonstration episodes, runs at 50 Hz instead of its original 10 Hz, and lacks an exploration bounding box. DAgger uses demonstrations plus the same intervention data.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 8–9, Figures 4–9 and captions; pp. 12–13, Appendices B–C
evidence.detail: Results are plotted rather than tabulated. Bar plots contain uncertainty whiskers but no definition is supplied; raw outcome counts and training seed count are not reported. Appendices add implementation descriptions rather than results tables.
